Notes

Body Fluid Electrolyte Distribution

KEY CONCEPT
Know which electrolytes predominate in each compartment — exact numbers are less important than intracellular vs extracellular recognition.
CompartmentPredominant Electrolytes
Intracellular fluid (ICF)Mainly K⁺ (~157 mEq/L), Mg²⁺, phosphate
Extracellular fluid (ECF)Mainly Na⁺, Cl⁻, with smaller amounts of K⁺, Ca²⁺; plasma also contains albumin/proteins
  • Potassium = main intracellular cation 426; chloride is mainly extracellular (K⁺, phosphate, Mg²⁺ are intracellular). 431 ×2

Notes

Increased Fluid Loss

Normal calculations must be increased when losses rise, from: fever, increased sweating/exercise, burns, or diarrhea/high-output GI losses.

RULES OF THUMB
Each 1°C fever rise → ~100–130 mL/day additional loss. Significant additional losses may increase requirement by roughly 500 mL–1 L/day or more. More watery GI output → loss of Na⁺ as well as K⁺.

Notes

IV Fluids

Common fluids: normal saline (0.9% NaCl), half-normal saline (0.45%), quarter-normal saline, Ringer's lactate/Hartmann's, D5-containing solutions. Know the composition of commonly used fluids and select according to the patient's volume/electrolyte problem.

  • Most common fluid problem in surgical patients → extracellular (volume) losses / hypovolemia. 437
  • Parkland = 4 ml × weight (kg) × %TBSA (2nd + 3rd degree only), half in the first 8 h from the time of burn, Ringer's lactate. 441
Notes

Common Crystalloid Composition

FluidComposition / Notes
Normal saline (0.9% NaCl)Relatively high Na⁺/Cl⁻ load; large volumes may produce a high chloride burden
Ringer's lactate / Hartmann'sNa⁺ ≈130, K⁺ ≈4, Cl⁻ ≈109, Ca²⁺ ≈2–3, Lactate/buffer ≈28 (all mEq/L) — more physiologically balanced than NS
Plasma-LyteAnother balanced crystalloid
Balanced solutions are closer to physiologic electrolyte composition and provide a buffering component.

Notes

Crystalloids vs Colloids

TypeCompositionDistribution / Effect
CrystalloidsWater + small dissolved electrolytes/molecules; e.g. normal saline, Ringer's lactate/Hartmann's, dextrose-containing solutionsReadily distribute through ECF — after isotonic infusion, ~25% remains intravascular / 75% enters interstitial space
ColloidsLarge molecules/proteins; e.g. blood, albumin, synthetic colloids (starch, gelatin, dextran)Cross capillary pores less readily → greater intravascular retention/oncotic effect
Albumin increases oncotic pressure → draws/retains fluid intravascularly, achieving volume expansion with less infused volume than crystalloid. May reduce total crystalloid volume required in selected patients, including septic shock.
  • The signs and symptoms of shock are determined by the amount of intravascular volume lost. 431

Notes

1. Resuscitation

For acute intravascular volume depletion threatening perfusion. Goal: rapidly restore circulating volume so blood can deliver O₂/nutrients. Urgent therapy — minutes to hours, not days.

FLUID CHOICE
Isotonic crystalloid (NS/Ringer's lactate) or selected colloid. No routine electrolyte additives during initial volume resuscitation — treat circulating volume first, not every individual electrolyte deficit simultaneously.
  • Fluid of choice for hypovolemia/hemorrhagic shock: isotonic crystalloid — Ringer's lactate (NS also keyed in one question). 441 442 434 ×2 431 ×3
  • Post-trauma ICU patient with hyperchloremic acidosis (Cl 115, HCO₃ 13) after resuscitation → bolus of Ringer's lactate (not more NS). 430
  • Burn resuscitation fluid → Ringer's lactate (Parkland) plus maintenance in children. 439 439

Notes

3. Maintenance

Replaces normal daily physiological losses when the patient cannot maintain oral intake (e.g. NPO). Approximate requirement: 35 mL/kg/day. Requires water ± glucose/electrolytes per normal requirements and labs. Reassess daily and return to oral intake ASAP.

Notes

2. Replacement

For existing or ongoing abnormal water/electrolyte losses (dehydration, diarrhea, stoma losses). Usually crystalloid, chosen according to what is being lost. May add specific depleted electrolytes: K⁺, Mg²⁺, phosphate. Unlike resuscitation, replacement specifically targets measured/estimated deficits.

  • Variceal hematemesis with hypotension: after the airway → crystalloid fluid resuscitation first, then endoscopy. 431 430 430
Notes

GI / Stoma Losses

REPLACEMENT RULE
Abnormal GI losses above expected baseline should be measured and replaced. High-output stoma/GI loss: replace approximately 1:1 — e.g. additional 500 mL loss → approximately 500 mL replacement. Use oral fluid if the patient can drink; otherwise generally an appropriate isotonic IV crystalloid. GI fluid losses can contain substantial Na⁺ and K⁺, particularly when watery.

Slide 36Fluid Balance in Surgical Patients
  • Surgery can alter the usual mechanisms.
  • Together, increased aldosterone and ADH generally make patients retain more water and salt, increase the tendency for edema, and become hypokalemic.
  • Fluid retention is enhanced by third spacing or sequestration in the surgical field.
  • The development of ileus may result in additional 1 to 3 L of fluid per day being sequestered in the bowel lumen, bowel wall, and peritoneal cavity.

IV Fluids & Electrolytes – SURG 453

Notes

Surgical Stress & Fluid Balance

STRESS RESPONSE
Surgery = major physiologic stress/tissue injury → ↑ ADH + aldosterone → water retention, Na⁺ retention, interstitial fluid expansion, edema. Excessive perioperative fluid administration worsens edema; bowel/tissue edema can make surgery and abdominal closure progressively more difficult.
Notes

Third-Space Sequestration

DEFINITION
Sequestration of fluid into interstitial/nonfunctional extracellular compartments without external fluid loss. Can occur after major surgery/stress even without bleeding, perforation, or obvious external fluid loss. Fluid may accumulate in bowel/interstitial tissues → bowel edema + ileus. Anesthetic agents and opioids/narcotics also worsen postoperative ileus, further impairing GI function and contributing to fluid/electrolyte disturbance.
  • Severe pancreatitis + sepsis: generalized edema despite large volumes of RL → third-space losses. 438 ×3 432 ×4
Slide 37Fluid Balance in Surgical Patients
  • In contrast to sodium retention, kidneys continue to excrete a minimum of 30 – 60 mEq/L of potassium daily, irrespective of serum potassium level.
  • Catabolism during 1st postoperative day releases sufficient potassium to meet daily requirements.
  • Beyond the 1st postoperative day, potassium supplementation is necessary. Glucose in the form of dextrose (D5) can be added to provide some calories while the patient is

NPO.

IV Fluids & Electrolytes – SURG 453

Notes

Post-op Day 1

Patient often remains NPO, so maintenance usually needs water, some glucose, appropriate Na⁺, and K⁺ supplementation.

POSTOPERATIVE K⁺ DEPLETION
May begin immediately but may not become evident on serum testing until POD1 or later (causes include urinary/GI K⁺ loss). Do not wait for marked hypokalemia before considering normal maintenance K⁺ replacement. Typical example: D5 + 0.45% NaCl + ~20 mEq K⁺ over 24 h, adjusted to labs.

Adjust saline concentration to serum Na⁺: lower Na⁺ → more isotonic saline may be needed; higher Na⁺ → more hypotonic/free-water component. Monitor fluid balance/electrolytes daily and transition to oral intake when possible.

Notes

Postoperative Fluid Management

Post-op Day 0 — Day of Surgery

Stress response → ADH/aldosterone-mediated Na⁺/water retention
Use isotonic maintenance fluid
Calculate by 4–2–1 rule / weight + 40
Avoid unnecessary over-resuscitation
LECTURE RECOMMENDATION
Do not exceed ~120 mL/hr, even in heavier adults, to avoid excessive edema/fluid retention.

Hypokalaemia

Slide 40
  • Occurs when serum K+ <3 mEq/L.
  • Treatment involves KCl IV infusion or orally.
  • THE MOST COMMON SURGICAL ABNORMALITY.
  • Should NOT be administered at a rate greater than 10-20 mmol/hr on peripheral IV and non-monitored settings.
  • If persistent hypokalaemia despite infusion replacement, check Mg2+ !

IV Fluids & Electrolytes – SURG 453

  • Peripheral IV K⁺ rate: 10–20 mmol/hr. 430 ×2
  • K⁺ 2.8 with flat T waves and U waves → IV potassium replacement 442; K⁺ 2.5 after laparotomy with NG drainage → IV infusion of KCl (never a bolus). 431 ×2
Notes

Treatment

Mild/stable: oral K⁺/potassium-rich foods when appropriate
Significant hospitalized hypokalemia → IV potassium replacement
Lecture rate: ~10–20 mEq/hr, depending on severity/access/monitoring
Follow exact pharmacy/hospital protocols
HIGH-YIELD SAFETY
IV K⁺ replacement is potentially dangerous — incorrect concentration/rate can cause a potentially fatal arrhythmia. Peripheral administration can cause pain/phlebitis/thrombophlebitis. Severe hypokalemia/high-rate replacement requires an appropriate IV line and cardiac monitoring.
Notes

Refractory Hypokalemia

HIGH-YIELD
If K⁺ will not correct → check Mg²⁺. Persistent hypomagnesemia makes K⁺ replacement ineffective.
  • Refractory hypokalemia → hypomagnesemia. 441

IV Fluids & Electrolytes – SURG 453

  • Suspected small-bowel obstruction (vomiting, distension) → first give IV fluids. 434
  • K⁺ 2.8 with muscle pain → cause among options: hyperaldosteronism. 441
  • Crohn's with 8–12 diarrhea episodes/day and flat T waves → hypokalemia. 439 ×3
  • Gastric fistula after sleeve gastrectomy → hypokalemia. 435 ×7
  • High-output small-bowel fistula / ileostomy / multiple laparotomies with fistula → normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate loss). 432 ×3 441 439 437
  • Normal-AG acidosis cause → renal tubular acidosis (hyperchloremia is a description, not a cause). 431
Notes

Potassium Disorders

Hypokalemia

Serum K⁺ below normal range; clinically important levels around <3–3.2 mEq/L. Very common postoperative/surgical electrolyte disturbance, especially around POD1.

CAUSES
Urinary postoperative K⁺ losses, GI losses, vomiting, poor intake/NPO state.
Notes

Vomiting

Gastric loss → loss of H⁺ + Cl⁻, volume depletion, and K⁺ depletion. Classic disturbance: hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.
  • Vomiting / NG suction / gastric outlet obstruction → hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis (paradoxical aciduria). 438 ×4 434 ×2 432 431 ×3 432 ×4
  • Metabolic alkalosis = loss of fixed acid or gain of bicarbonate (compensated by hypoventilation). 437
  • pH 7.5 with PCO₂ 25 and normal HCO₃ → respiratory alkalosis. 442

Hyperkalaemia

Slide 42
  • Diagnosis is established by increase serum K+ >6 mEq/L and ECG changes.
  • Causes include iatrogenic (increased K+ infusion in IV fluid), tissue injury, metabolic acidosis, renal failure, blood transfusion, and hemodialysis.
  • Arrythmia is the presentation !
  • Treatment: 1 ampule of D50% + 10 IU Insulin intravenously over 15 minutes, calcium (preferably gluconate), kayexalate oral/enemas, Lasix 20-40 mg IV, and dialysis if needed.

IV Fluids & Electrolytes – SURG 453

  • Hyperkalemia with ECG changes (wide QRS, tented T) → first IV calcium gluconate (calcium chloride in older keys). 442 ×2 434 ×6 429 428 426
  • Burn patient with K⁺ 7.1: the 441 version keyed calcium gluconate, the 438 version keyed insulin + dextrose; K⁺ 7.2 without ECG data → insulin + dextrose. 441 438 ×7 432
  • Trauma patient transferred from another hospital with low Na → most common cause iatrogenic (hypotonic fluids). 430
  • High-AG acidosis cause → severe hemorrhage (shock → lactic acidosis). 432 ×2
Notes

Hyperkalemia

DANGER
Potentially silent and fatal — serious cardiac toxicity may occur before prominent symptoms. Major danger = arrhythmia/cardiac arrest. Particularly important in renal failure/dialysis patients, who cannot adequately excrete K⁺.

Possible symptoms: muscle weakness/twitching, muscle discomfort, numbness/paresthesia.

Notes

Causes

Renal failure / impaired K⁺ excretion
Excessive or accidental IV K⁺ administration
Tissue/cellular injury — major surgery/trauma, muscle injury, rhabdomyolysis/crush injury
Stored blood transfusion (adds a K⁺ load)
Because K⁺ is predominantly intracellular, cell destruction → large K⁺ release into blood. Rhabdomyolysis also releases myoglobin → renal injury, further worsening K⁺ accumulation.
Notes

ECG

EXAM-IMPORTANT
ECG monitoring is essential. Hyperkalemia may cause peaked T waves, progressive conduction abnormalities, and heart block/serious arrhythmia. Recognize characteristic ECG abnormalities and prioritize immediate management.
  • Most serious consequence of hyperkalemia → arrhythmia. 438 ×3
  • Electrical injury with dark urine and high CK (rhabdomyolysis) → aggressive IV fluids with urine-output monitoring. 442
  • Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO₃). Na 132, Cl 95, HCO₃ 8 → 29; HCO₃ 15 → 22; Na 126, Cl 90, HCO₃ 11 → 25. 432 431 438 Final 434 ×2
Notes

Treatment

StepMechanism / AgentNotes
1. Stabilize myocardiumIV calcium gluconateGiven when severe hyperkalemia/ECG changes present; does not lower serum K⁺, protects the myocardium
2. Shift K⁺ intracellularlyInsulin + D50/glucoseInsulin drives K⁺ into cells; glucose prevents insulin-induced hypoglycemia. D50 alone does not meaningfully shift K⁺
3. Remove K⁺ from bodyLoop diuretic (e.g. furosemide), GI K⁺ binders, dialysisIncrease renal excretion when function permits; dialysis for severe/refractory cases with renal failure
DO NOT
Do not use potassium-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone to treat hyperkalemia.

Hypernatremia

Slide 44
  • Diagnosis is established when serum sodium > 145 mEq/L.
  • Primarily caused by high sodium infusion (e.g. 0.9% or 3% NaCl saline solutions).

Another but rare cause is hyperaldosteronism.

  • Patients with CHF, Cirrhosis, and nephrotic syndrome are prone to this complication
  • Symptoms and signs are similar to water excess.

Hyponatremia

Slide 47
  • Causes are hyperglycemia, and excessive IV sodium-free fluid administration (e.g. D5W).
  • The Sodium Correction for Hyperglycemia calculates the actual sodium level in patients with hyperglycemia.

Sodium Correction = measured Na + [(glucose level - 100) x 0.016]

  • Could be volume overload, normo, low volume.
  • Hyponatremia with volume overload usually indicates impaired renal ability to excrete sodium

IV Fluids & Electrolytes – SURG 453

  • Type 1 DM with glucose 37 and Na 124 → pseudohyponatremia (dilutional from hyperglycemia). 432
Slide 48Hyponatremia
  • In mild to moderate deficit, administer the calculated Na+ needs in an isotonic solution.
  • In severe hyponatremia (Na+ less than 120 mEq/L): hypertonic sodium solution.

Fluids, Electrolytes, and Acid-Base

Fluids and electrolytes
  • Body water distribution and composition
  • Total Body Water Distribution: constitutes approximately 59%-60% of body mass. The percentage varies based on age, gender, and body composition, being higher in men compared to women, in children compared to adults, and in individuals with normal body weight compared to obese individuals.
  • TBW is divided into:
    • Intracellular fluid (ICF): Comprising 30%-40% of body mass (~ two-thirds of TBW).
    • Extracellular fluid (ECF): Constituting 15%-20% of body mass (~ one-third of TBW), further subdivided into:
    • Interstitial fluid: 12%-16% of total body mass (~ 80% of ECF).
    • Intravascular fluid: 3%-4% of total body mass (~ 20% of ECF), with one-fifth proximal to arterioles and four- fifths distal.
  • Electrolyte Composition The composition of fluids varies between compartments:
    • Intracellular fluid: Predominantly contains potassium (K+), balanced by phosphate (PO4³⁻) and negatively charged proteins.
    • Extracellular fluid: Primarily contains sodium (Na+), balanced by chloride (Cl⁻) and bicarbonate (HCO3⁻).
    • Intravascular fluid: Higher protein concentration (mainly albumin) than interstitial fluid, contributing to colloid osmotic pressure, which regulates fluid distribution between ECF compartments.
  • Fluid Movement and Regulation The exchange of water across compartments is driven by:
    • Colloid osmotic pressure: Primarily determined by plasma proteins.
    • Hydrostatic pressure: Governs capillary fluid movement, as described by the Starling equation.
    • Osmolality regulation: Maintained around 290 mOsm/kg through water intake and excretion.
  • Renal Regulation of Fluid Balance The kidneys play a crucial role in maintaining volume and osmolality by modulating sodium (Na+) and water reabsorption:
    • Sodium Handling:
    • 60%-70% of filtered Na+ is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule.
    • 20%-30% is reabsorbed in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.
    • 5%-10% is reabsorbed in the distal tubule and collecting ducts.
    • Sodium balance is tightly regulated by hormones such as aldosterone and natriuretic peptides.
  • Water Regulation:
    • Antidiuretic hormone (ADH): Released by the posterior pituitary in response to increased serum osmolality.
    • ADH facilitates water reabsorption by inserting aquaporin channels in the collecting ducts, resulting in concentrated urine.
    • In the absence of ADH, water is lost through dilute urine.
    • At high levels, ADH also induces vasoconstriction of arterioles.
  • Daily requirements
  • Fluids: 35cc/kg/day
  • Na: 1-3 mEq/kg/day
  • K: 1 mEq/kg/day
  • Ca: 10-15 mEq/day
  • Mg: 8-20 mEq/day
  • PO4: 20-40 mmol/day
  • Normal daily fluid loss
  • Conditions with increased water requirement
  • Fever
  • Sweating
  • Burns
  • Tachypnea
  • Polyuria
  • Surgical drains
  • Ongoing significant GI loss (stomas)
  • Water requirements increase by 100-150 ml/day for each 1 C increase in body temperature

    • Isotonic fluid at maintenance rate (4/2/1 rule or weight + age), but not exceeding 120cc/h

Hypovolemia
  • Etiology
    • Hypovolemia is a common condition in surgical patients caused by the loss of isotonic fluids. Key causes include:
    • Hemorrhage
    • Gastrointestinal losses (e.g., gastric suctioning, vomiting, diarrhea)
    • Fluid sequestration in the gut (e.g., bowel obstruction, ileus, enteric fistula)
    • Burns and excessive diuretic therapy
    • Sweating (especially in resource-poor settings)
  • Presentation
    • Diagnosis relies on history, physical examination, and lab tests, though mild-to-moderate hypovolemia is difficult to detect, especially in the elderly and young children. Physical signs include:
    • Sensitive indicators: Dry oral/nasal mucosa, longitudinal tongue furrows
    • Specific indicators: Increased capillary refill time, weak speech, extremity weakness, dry axilla, postural hypotension
    • Severe hypovolemia: Heart rate increase of ≥30 bpm upon standing or postural dizziness preventing standing (91–100% sensitivity)
  • Laboratory findings:
    • Elevated BUN:Cr ratio due to prerenal azotemia (though also seen in renal failure and GI bleeding)
  • Treatment
    • Treatment involves IV administration of isotonic fluids. Recent studies favor balanced crystalloids (e.g., lactated Ringer’s) over normal saline due to a lower risk of hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis and kidney failure.
    • Electrolyte imbalances should be corrected alongside fluid resuscitation.
    • Caution in renal or heart failure patients to avoid fluid overload.
    • If untreated, hypovolemia can progress to circulatory collapse and shock.
    • Extra:
    • If Na > 145 mEq/l, give 0.45 % NS
    • If Na > 160 mEq/l, give 5 % Dextrose with water
    • Gastrointestinal and intraoperative loss should be replaced in a ratio of 1:1
Hypervolemia
  • Etiology
    • Hypervolemia is common in surgical patients and often results from excessive administration of colloid and crystalloid fluids during shock treatment. Other contributing factors include:
    • Postoperative ADH secretion: In response to a nonphysiological stimuli, leading to sodium (Na⁺) and water retention. ADH levels usually normalize within 2–3 days, causing autodiuresis.
    • Heart failure: Reduces the body's ability to compensate for increased intravascular volume.
    • Liver disease: Decreases metabolism of ADH and aldosterone, raising the intravascular volume set point.
    • Renal disease: Impairs volume regulation mechanisms.
    • Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH Secretion (SIADH): Leads to excess water retention due to inappropriate ADH release, commonly associated with:
    • Traumatic brain injuries, tumors, or abscesses
    • Pneumonia and lung abscesses
    • Paraneoplastic syndrome (e.g., small-cell lung cancer)
    • Drugs: Morphine, cyclophosphamide, vincristine
  • Presentation
    • Hypervolemia is often diagnosed based on patient history and physical examination. Key signs include:
    • Hypertension
    • Decreased arterial oxygen saturation & basilar crackles
    • Jugular venous distension (JVD)
    • Dependent edema (soft tissue swelling in lower limbs)
    • Gallop rhythms on cardiac auscultation
    • Rapid weight gain
  • Treatment
    • Diuretics (e.g., loop diuretics) are the first-line treatment to reduce excess fluid.
    • Hemodialysis may be required in extreme cases (e.g., renal failure).
    • Mechanical ventilation is necessary for severe pulmonary edema or CHF leading to respiratory failure.
  • Electrolyte disorders
Hyponatremia
  • Etiology
    • Hyponatremia results from relative water gain rather than absolute sodium (Na⁺) loss. Total body sodium may be decreased, normal, or increased.
  • Common causes in surgical patients:
    • Postoperative ADH secretion in response to:
    • Pain, nausea, vomiting
    • Opiate use
    • Positive-pressure ventilation
    • Rapid administration of hypotonic fluids
    • Severe hyperglycemia (osmotic shift of water from intracellular to extracellular compartments)
    • Other conditions:
    • Cerebral salt-wasting syndrome
    • Liver disease
    • Congestive heart failure
    • Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH)
  • Presentation
    • Symptoms vary based on the rate of sodium decline:
    • Acute hyponatremia (rapid drop in Na⁺ levels) → Central nervous system (CNS) dysfunction due to brain swelling (Monro-Kellie hypothesis).
    • Severe cases (Na⁺ < 120 mmol/L): Mental status changes, obtundation, coma, seizures → medical emergency
    • Chronic hyponatremia (slow decline in Na⁺) → Often asymptomatic but may require correction if associated with increased intracranial pressure.
  • Treatment
    • Chronic hyponatremia:
    • Free water restriction and salt tablets
    • If severe (< 120 mmol/L), use 3% normal saline
    • Slow sodium correction to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome (4–6 mEq/L per day).
    • Acute hyponatremia with CNS symptoms:
    • More rapid correction with hypertonic saline until symptoms improve, then shift to conservative management.
    • No consensus on the exact correction rate, but recommendations suggest not exceeding 8 mmol/L per day, starting with 1–2 mmol/L per hour in severe cases.
    • Sodium correction does not replace pharmacologic intervention in seizure patients.
  • Severe cases with CNS disturbances require ICU admission for close monitoring and rapid intervention to avoid potentially fatal complications.
Hypernatremia
  • Etiology
    • Hypernatremia occurs due to free water loss rather than an absolute sodium (Na⁺) gain. Total body sodium may be increased, normal, or decreased.
  • Common causes include:
    • Lack of access to water (e.g., preverbal infants, bedbound, incapacitated patients)
    • Diabetes insipidus (deficient ADH function leading to excessive water loss)
    • High fevers
    • Inadequate water intake with enteral feeding
    • Iatrogenic hypernatremia is used in traumatic brain injury treatment to:
    • Reduce cerebral edema
    • Lower intracranial pressure
    • Increase cerebral perfusion pressure
  • Presentation
    • Lethargy and fatigue
    • Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes
    • Seizures and coma (in severe cases)
  • Treatment
    • Symptomatic hypernatremia requires free water replacement:
    • IV 5% dextrose in water (D5W)
    • Enteral free water administration (if possible)
    • Slow correction is crucial to prevent cerebral edema and encephalopathy:
    • If hypernatremia develops over hours, correct it at 1–2 mmol/L per hour, targeting normonatremia within 24 hours.
    • If hypernatremia developed gradually, correct at a slower rate (≤0.5 mmol/L per hour).
  • Severe hypernatremia with CNS manifestations requires ICU admission for close monitoring and controlled correction.
Hypokalemia
  • Etiology
    • Hypokalemia in surgical patients is primarily due to total body potassium (K⁺) depletion, commonly caused by:
    • Gastrointestinal losses (e.g., vomiting, diarrhea)
    • Excessive diuretic use
    • Prolonged malnutrition, particularly in alcoholic patients
    • Prolonged alkalosis leading to paradoxical aciduria where the nephron conserves K⁺ at the expense of H⁺, maintaining alkalosis instead of correcting it.
  • Presentation
    • Decreased muscle contractility, which can progress to diaphragmatic paralysis.
    • ECG changes:
    • Flattened or inverted T-waves
    • Prominent U-waves
    • Cardiac arrhythmias can be life-threatening.
  • Treatment
    • Acute hypokalemia → Parenteral potassium (KCl) supplementation (at no more than 10-20 mmol/h on peripheral IV line and non-monitored setting).
    • IMP!!! Refractory hypokalemia → Check and correct hypomagnesemia, as low magnesium can prevent potassium correction.
    • Chronic or mild hypokalemia (without neuromuscular or cardiac symptoms) → Oral potassium supplementation (dietary changes or oral potassium chloride).
Hyperkalemia
  • Etiology
    • Hyperkalemia in surgical patients is often due to excessive potassium (K⁺) accumulation from:
    • Crush injuries, burns, and catabolic states (cellular breakdown releases intracellular K⁺)
    • Renal insufficiency (impaired K⁺ excretion)
    • Adrenal insufficiency (decreased aldosterone leads to K⁺ retention)
    • Excessive K⁺ administration
    • Acidosis, where H⁺ is exchanged for intracellular K⁺, causing K⁺ to move into the extracellular space
    • Pseudohyperkalemia from hemolysis during venipuncture, requiring repeat testing for confirmation
  • Presentation
    • Hyperkalemia is often asymptomatic until severe, when life- threatening cardiac arrhythmias develop. ECG findings progress as hyperkalemia worsens:
    • Flattened P-waves
    • Peaked T-waves
    • PR prolongation
    • QRS widening → Requires immediate intervention, as it indicates imminent ventricular fibrillation.
  • Treatment
    • Hyperkalemia (K⁺ ≥ 6.5 mmol/L) is a medical emergency requiring immediate intervention and continuous ECG monitoring.
    • Acute management (temporary K⁺ shift into cells):
    • IV 50% dextrose + 10 units regular insulin
    • Calcium gluconate (stabilizes myocardium, prevents arrhythmias)
    • Inhaled β-agonists (e.g., albuterol)
    • Sodium bicarbonate is not proven beneficial
    • Definitive K⁺ removal from the body:
    • Loop or thiazide diuretics (if renal function is intact)
    • Hemodialysis (if renal failure is present)
    • Sodium sulfonate (slow enteral K⁺ removal in mild cases where K⁺ is < 6.5 mmol/L )
    • Address underlying causes to prevent recurrence of hyperkalemia.
Hypomagnesemia
  • Etiology
    • Hypomagnesemia commonly occurs in surgical patients due to magnesium depletion, often caused by:
    • Malnutrition, particularly in alcoholism
    • Gastrointestinal losses (e.g., prolonged diarrhea)
    • Diuretic or aminoglycoside use
    • Calcium imbalances (hypercalcemia or hypocalcemia)
    • Hypophosphatemia
  • Presentation
    • Refractory hypokalemia despite parenteral K⁺ administration is a key sign.
    • Other symptoms include:
    • Sedation and muscle paralysis
    • Tetany and seizures
    • Coma (in severe cases)
  • Treatment
    • Parenteral magnesium (Mg²⁺) administration is preferred over oral supplementation, as oral magnesium acts as a cathartic (induces diarrhea).
Hypermagnesemia
  • Etiology
    • Hypermagnesemia is rare in surgical patients but can occur in acute renal failure, where magnesium excretion is impaired.
  • Presentation
    • Magnesium acts as a calcium (Ca²⁺) antagonist, leading to:
    • Lethargy and weakness
    • Diminished deep tendon reflexes
    • Cardiac arrhythmias which are the most serious manifestations:
    • Peaked T-waves
    • QRS widening
    • Progression to complete heart block, severe arrhythmias, and asystole (cardiac arrest)
  • Treatment
    • Mild cases (due to supplementation) → Stop magnesium intake and monitor.
    • Severe cases with ECG changes:
    • IV calcium gluconate to counteract magnesium's calcium-antagonizing effects on neuromuscular function.
    • Loop or thiazide diuretics to enhance magnesium excretion (if renal function is intact).
    • Hemodialysis in severe cases or renal failure.
Hypocalcemia
  • Etiology
    • Hypocalcemia in surgical patients is often due to:
    • Hypoparathyroidism (either congenital or iatrogenic, e.g., after thyroid or parathyroid surgery)
    • Hypothyroidism
    • Pancreatitis
    • Renal insufficiency
    • Crush injuries
    • Severe soft tissue infections (e.g., necrotizing fasciitis)
  • Presentation
    • Hypocalcemia primarily affects neuromuscular function, causing:
    • Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes
    • Chvostek’s sign (facial muscle spasm upon tapping the facial nerve)
    • Muscle cramps and abdominal pain
    • Severe cases: Tetany and cardiac arrhythmias
  • Treatment
    • Check whole-blood pH and correct alkalosis if present.
    • Severe or symptomatic hypocalcemia (e.g., prolonged QT interval, rapid calcium drop):
    • IV calcium administration is required.
    • Mild or asymptomatic cases:
    • Enteral calcium supplementation is sufficient.
    • Chronic hypoparathyroidism or hypothyroidism:
    • Chronic vitamin D and calcium supplementation
    • Aluminum hydroxide may be needed to reduce phosphate (PO₄³⁻) absorption from the gut.
Hypercalcemia
  • Etiology
    • Hypercalcemia in surgical patients is often due to:
    • Primary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism
    • Hyperthyroidism
    • Bone metastases from cancer
    • Paraneoplastic syndromes (e.g., secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide)
    • Thiazide diuretic use
  • Presentation
    • Acute hypercalcemia symptoms include:
    • Gastrointestinal: Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, polydipsia, polyuria, constipation, dyspepsia
    • Neurological: Depression, confusion, memory loss, psychosis, stupor, coma
    • Cardiac: Arrhythmias
    • Renal: Nephrolithiasis
    • Chronic hypercalcemia complications:
    • Skeletal: Osteoporosis, osteomalacia, osteitis fibrosa cystica
    • Pancreatitis
    • Calciphylaxis (calcific uremic arteriolopathy):
    • Serious and often fatal
    • Causes arteriole calcification, leading to skin ischemia, necrosis, and ulceration
    • High risk of infection, morbidity, and mortality
  • Treatment
    • Initial treatment (for patients with intact kidney function):
    • IV normal saline hydration (1–3 days) to enhance calcium excretion
    • Monitor urine output (target: 2–3 mL/kg/h)
  • Severe cases: (Ca > 14 mg/dl with ECG changes)
    • IV calcitonin and bisphosphonates
    • Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) to promote calciuresis
    • Hemodialysis (if hypercalcemia is severe or due to renal failure)
  • Long-term management:
    • Bisphosphonates for malignancy-related hypercalcemia
    • Parathyroidectomy for hyperparathyroidism (elective unless patient is in a hypercalcemic crisis that is refractory to medical treatment)
Hypophosphatemia
  • Etiology
    • Hypophosphatemia is commonly seen in malnourished patients, especially those with:
    • Chronic alcoholism
    • Excessive antacid consumption (which binds phosphate)
    • Post-liver resection
  • A critical but often overlooked cause is refeeding syndrome, which occurs when a severely malnourished patient resumes eating after ≥5 days of fasting.
  • Onset: Typically, within 4 days of refeeding.
  • Presentation
    • Hypophosphatemia causes muscular and neurological dysfunction, including:
    • Muscle weakness
    • Diplopia (double vision)
    • Depressed cardiac output
    • Respiratory depression (diaphragmatic weakness)
    • Confusion, delirium, coma, and death
    • Rhabdomyolysis (rare but possible)
    • Ventilator dependency due to failure to replenish ATP stores for respiratory muscles
  • Treatment
    • Severe hypophosphatemia is a medical emergency requiring IV sodium phosphate (Na₂PO₄) or potassium phosphate (K₂PO₄) based on the patient’s electrolyte profile.
    • Mild cases can be treated with oral phosphate supplements or phosphate-rich foods (e.g., milk).
Hyperphosphatemia
  • Etiology
    • Hyperphosphatemia is uncommon in surgical patients but can occur in:
    • Severe renal disease (impaired phosphate excretion)
    • Severe trauma (tissue breakdown releasing phosphate)
  • Presentation
    • Usually asymptomatic
    • Can cause hypocalcemia due to calcium phosphate precipitation and tissue deposition
  • Treatment
    • Diuresis to enhance phosphate excretion
    • Phosphate binders (e.g., aluminum hydroxide) to reduce intestinal absorption
    • Hemodialysis for severe cases or renal failure
  • Acid-base disorders
